Pratima Gurung1,2, Peter S. Back 1,2, Ilzat Ali 1,3, Gabrielle M. Hernandez 1,3 & Jeffrey D. Dvorin 1,2

The apical polar ring (APR) is a defining cytoskeletal structure in apicomplexan parasites, critical for parasite morphology and host cell invasion. However, its molecular composition and function remain elusive in Plasmodium falciparum. Here we identify and characterize PfAPR3 as an APR-resident protein. Conditional knockout of PfAPR3 reveals its essential role in asexual replication. PfAPR3-knockout parasites contact host red blood cells but fail to form a tight junction, resulting in a complete block in invasion. Using PfAPR3 as bait, we identify three additional APR proteins (PfAPR4, PfCHAKRA and PfAPR5) and delineate APR biogenesis with ultrastructure expansion microscopy. Unlike PfAPR3, PfCHAKRA is critical for cytoskeletal network organization. Iterative ultrastructure expansion microscopy further shows PfCHAKRA at the basal APR until mid-schizogony, with PfAPR3 exhibiting dual apical–basal ring localization during schizogony. These findings define the molecular architecture and function of the APR in P. falciparum and have implications for understanding parasite host cell infection.

The apicomplexan parasite Plasmodium falciparum causes the deadliest form of human malaria1, replicating asexually in human red blood cells (RBCs) via schizogony to produce dozens of daughter merozoites per cycle2. Apicomplexan parasites possess a characteristic apical complex3–6, containing the apical polar ring (APR), secretory organelles (rhoptries and micronemes) and, in some apicomplexans, a conoid3,7. The APR is a central component in apicomplexans, identified by electron microscopy >50 years ago3,4,8–12. The apical complex is critical for parasite shape, egress and invasion. In P. falciparum, the APR contains three concentric rings (diameters: 180 nm, 240 nm and 370 nm). The two top rings are connected by a 34-unit bridge structure, while the basal ring is the largest and thickest6. This basal ring is connected to the parasite’s cytoskeleton, known as the inner membrane complex (IMC) and subpellicular microtubules (SPMTs)6,13–15. During schizogony, the IMC forms at the apical end of developing merozoites, later expanding and enveloping them. The APR marks the apex of the IMC and is hypothesized to anchor the SPMTs in apicomplexans4,6,11,12,15–20. Recent studies suggest that the centrosome-associated microtubule organizing center nucleates

microtubules, which are later handed off to the APR10,11,21,22. The APR and its associated cytoskeleton are crucial for parasite shape, cell division and invasion. Despite its prominence in invasive stages6,13,23,24, the molecular components and function of the P. falciparum APR remain incompletely understood. The APR has been extensively studied in Toxoplasma gondii4,6,11,12,17,20,25–28. Only 5 of 11 known T. gondii APR components (APR2/ TGME49_227000, APR3/TGME49_208340, APR4/TGME49_219500, APR5/TGME49_299190 and APR7/TGME49_320030) have Plasmodium orthologues4,12. In Plasmodium berghei, PbAPR1/PBANKA_0907700 and PbAPR2/PBANKA_1334800, orthologues of TgAPR3 and TgAPR7, localize at the apical end of ookinetes4. Recently, PyAPR2 and two associated proteins were localized to the APR in Plasmodium yoelii18. PyAPR2 depletion impairs APR formation and SPMT anchorage, preventing mosquito transmission. However, no APR proteins have been identified in P. falciparum, and the biological function of the APR in human malaria parasites remains unknown. PfAPR3 and its interactors are essential for asexual parasite replication We induced PfAPR3 gene excision with rapamycin and confirmed excision by PCR and western blot (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). PfAPR3-knockout (PfAPR3-KO) parasites showed a 98 ± 0.6% growth reduction in one replication cycle (Fig. 2a). Monitoring egress and invasion every 4 h (44–56 hpi) by Hemacolor staining revealed that PfAPR3-KO parasites showed normal egress but failed to invade new RBCs, remaining adjacent to the RBC surface (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Collectively, these results show that PfAPR3 is essential for merozoite invasion of RBCs. We tested whether PfAPR3-interacting proteins are essential by inducing knockdown via anhydrotetracycline (ATc) removal. Without ATc, TetR binds target mRNA aptamer arrays, and DOZI sequesters them into stress granules40,41. Without ATc, PfAPR4 levels decreased to 7.8 ± 2.7% of the ATc control, PfCHAKRA to 3.2 ± 0.8% and PfAPR5 to 29.6 ± 11.6% (Extended Data Fig. 2h–j). Replication assays revealed significant growth defects: PfAPR4 (92 ± 3% reduction), PfCHAKRA (98 ± 1% reduction) and PfAPR5 (73 ± 2% reduction) within one cycle (Fig. 2b–d), showing that all three proteins are individually essential.

PfAPR3 is dispensable for IMC formation but modulates SPMT organization U-ExM analysis revealed that IMC formation proceeded normally in PfAPR3-KO parasites. However, unlike wild-type (WT) schizonts that produce individual merozoites, PfAPR3-KO schizonts frequently generated a single multinucleated daughter-cell agglomerate enclosed by IMC, indicating defective segmentation (Extended Data Fig. 4a). To assess SPMT formation and organization, mature parasites were arrested before parasitophorous vacuolar membrane rupture with the protein kinase G inhibitor, ML10 (ref. 42), and stained with ɑ-tubulin. SPMTs formed and anchored to the APR in both WT and PfAPR3-KO parasites. WT parasites showed paired, nearly parallel SPMTs (average angle of 14 ± 1.5° between them), aligned along one side of each merozoite. By contrast, PfAPR3-KO merozoites showed a significantly increased angle between SPMTs (47 ± 2°), with >50% showing disorganized or non-parallel SPMT arrangements (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). These data show that PfAPR3 is required for proper SPMT alignment. NHS-ester staining confirmed intact apical–basal polarity in PfAPR3-KO parasites, with rhoptries apically positioned, and the basal complex at the basal end (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). The dense APR structure was preserved, indicating that PfAPR3 is dispensable for APR assembly. Thus, PfAPR3 is dispensable for IMC biogenesis, apical polarity and APR formation, but essential for SPMT alignment and merozoite segmentation.

PfAPR3 loss prevents tight junction formation We analysed invasion in synchronized PfAPRDiCre parasites (±rapamycin) after release from ML10-induced arrest, using IFA, live-cell differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy and U-ExM. Merozoite invasion of RBCs proceeds through pre-invasion (attachment and reorientation), internalization (tight junction formation and entry) and ring-stage establishment43–45. During invasion, merozoites induce changes in the RBC cytoskeleton to modulate membrane deformability: pre-invasion causes mild deformation, while internalization induces pronounced, reversible echinocytosis, characterized by a spiky membrane morphology45,46. Time-lapse DIC microscopy revealed that WT merozoites efficiently completed all invasion stages and induced characteristic RBC echinocytosis (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Video 1). PfAPR3 is essential for host cell invasion, while PfCHAKRA controls APR biogenesis and cytoskeletal organization. Together, our findings define the molecular framework of APR biogenesis and function.

Results PfAPR3 is an APR-resident protein in P. falciparum We used rodent malaria APR-resident proteins to identify P. falciparum orthologues4,18,29. We identified PfAPR3 (PF3D7_1141300) as a potential candidate following a BLAST search of the P. falciparum genome30. PfAPR3 shows 44.9% sequence identity with PbAPR1/PBANKA_0907700, which is the orthologue of TgAPR3 (refs. 4,12; Extended Data Fig. 1). To avoid confusion, we named the P. falciparum proteins similar to their T. gondii orthologues throughout. PfAPR3 is ~111 kDa (1,012 amino acids) in size and contains a pleckstrin homology-like domain at residues 876–977. Transposon screens predict that it is essential for asexual replication31,32. To investigate the role of PfAPR3, we generated an inducible knockout strain (referred to as PfAPR3DiCre) in the NF54DiCre(pfs47) background, which expresses split dimerizable Cre recombinase33. We replaced the native PfAPR3 gene locus with a loxP-flanked, codon-altered PfAPR3 tagged at the C-terminus with three copies of the haemagglutinin (HA) epitope (Extended Data Fig. 2a). The strain was verified by PCR, sequencing and western blot (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Immunofluorescence assays (IFAs) revealed that PfAPR3 is undetectable before schizogony, when it appears as a distinct ring-like structure at the apical end of developing and mature merozoites (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 3a). To determine the timing of PfAPR3 expression, we co-stained with PfGAP45, an IMC-associated protein that localizes to the forming IMC in early schizonts (~5 nuclei, 40 h post-invasion (hpi)) and later surrounds mature merozoites34,35. IFA showed that PfAPR3 expression coincides temporally with PfGAP45 and appears at the apex of PfGAP45 in merozoites (Fig. 1a). PfAPR3 localizes apical to PfAMA1, a micronemal marker36. This suggests that PfAPR3 resides at the extreme apical tip of the merozoites, possibly at the APR (Fig. 1b). Ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) with N-hydroxysuccinimide Alexa Fluor 405 (NHS-ester) staining, which labels the protein-dense APR34,37, showed that PfAPR3 colocalizes with the APR as a discrete ring. The apical ends of SPMTs are positioned beneath both PfAPR3 and the NHS-ester-stained APR (Fig. 1c). These findings establish PfAPR3 as a bona fide resident of the APR in P. falciparum.

PfAPR3-interacting proteins (PfAPR4, PfCHAKRA,PfCHAKRA and PfAPR5) Co-immunoprecipitation using α-HA on late-stage PfAPR3DiCre schizonts followed by mass spectrometry identified 49 high-confidence interactors (≥10-fold enrichment and ≥10 unique peptides across replicates; Supplementary Table 1). We prioritized three uncharacterized candidates—PF3D7_1128900, PF3D7_1138000 and PF3D7_1307900—that are predicted to be essential for parasite replication30,38. PF3D7_1128900 (73.8 kDa) is the orthologue of TgAPR4 (refs. 4,12); thus, we named it PfAPR4. PF3D7_1138000 is a large (335.7 kDa) Plasmodium-specific protein of unknown function. We named it cytoskeletal hook apical key ring-associated protein (PfCHAKRA). PF3D7_1307900 (105 kDa) contains a B-box-type zinc-finger domain39 with 25% identity over this domain to TgAPR5; we named it PfAPR5. We generated dual-transgenic strains (PfGOIiKD) by fusing ten copies of the TetR-binding aptamer and a spaghetti monster V5 (smV5) tag to the 3′ end of each gene in the PfAPR3DiCre background (and PfAPR5 was also tagged with smHA separately in NF54DiCre(pfs47) parasites). These parasites also express TetR-DOZI, a fusion protein between the TetR binding protein and development of zygote inhibited (DOZI). All parasite strains were verified by PCR and western blot (Extended Data Fig. 2d–j). IFAs showed all candidates localized as rings at the merozoite apex, apical to PfGAP45 (Fig. 1d). U-ExM confirmed alignment with the NHS-ester-stained APR (Fig. 1e). Reverse

Because successful invasion requires secretion of micronemes and rhoptries, we tested whether PfAPR3 influences these secretory events. Western blot analysis of culture supernatants detected similar levels of micronemal release of PfEBA175 in WT and PfAPR3-KO (109 ± 24% of WT). By contrast, PfRh2a (rhoptry marker) secretion was significantly reduced in PfAPR3-KO (72 ± 13% of WT) (Fig. 3d). Schizont expression levels were unchanged for both proteins (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h), indicating that PfAPR3 selectively affects rhoptry secretion without altering PfRh2a production. We next examined whether PfAPR3 ablation affects PfAMA1 translocation. PfAMA1 is proteolytically processed and translocated to the merozoite surface during egress, a prerequisite for invasion36,49. IFA on mid- and E64-arrested schizonts revealed normal PfAMA1 expression and merozoite-surface translocation in PfAPR3-KO parasites (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that PfAPR3 does not alter PfAMA1 expression or translocation. Given normal PfAMA1 translocation, we next investigated tight junction (TJ) formation by tracking PfRON4 (a TJ complex component) during invasion44,50,51. In WT parasites, PfRON4 redistributes from the apical rhoptry neck to an arc or ring-like configuration, observed as paired puncta in single z-slices, corresponding to the TJ and then disperses along the parasitophorous vacuolar membrane after invasion. In PfAPR3-KO parasites, PfRON4 remained confined to a single apical focus throughout merozoite attachment and reorientation, with no evidence of TJ formation or characteristic redistribution (Fig. 3e). These results suggest that PfAPR3 is required for TJ formation during invasion. To confirm this, we analysed rhoptry discharge using PfRAP1 (a rhoptry bulb marker52–55). In early invasion, PfRAP1 localized apically

as a small circle in both WT (12 ± 29%) and KO (93 ± 5%) parasites. In mid-invasion, WT and CytoD-arrested controls (12 ± 12%) showed a characteristic C-shaped or doughnut-shaped PfRAP1 pattern, while PfAPR3-KO parasites showed only faint, distorted, doughnut-like patterns (6 ± 1%), indicating limited rhoptry release. They never showed the extensive PfRAP1 spreading along the RBC surface characteristic of R1-peptide-treated parasites54. By late invasion, PfRAP1 localized around the successfully invaded merozoites only in WT parasites (76 ± 24%), confirming failed rhoptry discharge in PfAPR3-KO. Schizont PfRAP1 expression was unchanged, establishing that PfAPR3 selectively impairs rhoptry discharge during invasion (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). U-ExM visualization during invasion stages captured all invasion stages in WT parasites, including rare mid-invasion in WT parasites but only attached and reoriented stages in PfAPR3-KO parasites, with no evidence of internalization (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Collectively, these findings establish that PfAPR3 is essential for post-reorientation invasion by influencing secretion of rhoptry proteins that are required for TJ formation and successful invasion.

PfAPR4 or PfAPR5 deficiency has similar phenotypic consequences as PfAPR3 deficiency To assess the role of PfAPR4 and PfAPR5 during schizogony, we analysed their depletion using U-ExM. PfAPR4- and PfAPR5-deficient parasites showed normal IMC formation and apical polarity but displayed moderate segmentation defects similar to PfAPR3-KO with abnormal multinucleated daughter-cell agglomerates (Extended Data Figs. 2h,j and 6a,c). Some PfAPR5-deficient parasites retained normal morphology, probably reflecting incomplete protein knockdown (30% residual protein) (Extended Data Fig. 2j). PfAPR4-deficient parasites showed disorganized SPMT alignment in >50% of daughter cells, similar to PfAPR3-KO, while PfAPR5-deficient parasites showed less severe SPMT disorganization (Extended Data Fig. 6b,d). On the basis of these similarities to PfAPR3-KO, we infer that PfAPR4 and PfAPR5 are similarly required for invasion but did not perform independent invasion assays.

PfCHAKRA coordinates apical–basal polarity and cytoskeletal organization during schizogony Unlike PfAPR4 and PfAPR5, PfCHAKRA knockdown produced strong morphologic abnormalities in schizonts. In control schizonts, each daughter merozoite was individually enclosed by the IMC (PfGAP45). PfCHAKRA-deficient schizonts showed PfGAP45 enveloping multiple merozoites, forming multinucleated ‘megazoite’ agglomerates, along with occasional PfGAP45 zoids lacking nuclei (Fig. 4a). This segmentation defect was confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (Fig. 4b). PfCHAKRA depletion disrupted apical organelle organization. The APR was largely absent, with only occasional NHS-ester-stained APR (2 or 3 per parasite) remnants visible, probably owing to incomplete knockdown (3 ± 1% residual PfCHAKRA protein; Extended Data Fig. 2i). While control schizonts consistently showed two rhoptries per merozoite associated with the APR, PfCHAKRA-deficient parasites contained single, detached or clustered rhoptries lacking the APR ring or apical positioning (Fig. 4a,b). These findings show that PfCHAKRA is essential for APR formation and rhoptry organization. To examine whether the APR anchors SPMTs, we analysed SPMT organization following PfCHAKRA knockdown. U-ExM revealed excessively long, disorganized microtubules in PfCHAKRA-deficient parasites compared with controls. Notably, these abnormal microtubules were confirmed as SPMTs by polyglutamylated tubulin (α-polyE) staining at their apical ends, distinguishing them from mitotic spindle microtubules13,34,56,57 (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Given that SPMTs nucleate at the centriolar plaque (CP)22,34,56,57, we assessed whether SPMT nucleation is affected by APR loss. PfAPR3-interacting proteins show distinct APR localization dependencies Because all four APR proteins are individually essential, we investigated whether they depend on one another for correct localization. We used dual transgenic parasite lines (PfAPR4iKD, PfCHAKRAiKD and PfAPR5iKD), each expressing smV5-tagged PfAPR3-interacting partners, to analyse their colocalization with PfAPR3 (ɑ-HA) under three conditions by U-ExM: (1) both proteins present, (2) partner protein depleted and (3) PfAPR3 knocked out.

PfAPR4–PfAPR3 mutual dependency. U-ExM revealed that PfAPR4 and PfAPR3 colocalized closely (Pearson’s R = 0.70). In PfAPR4-deficient parasites, PfAPR3 staining was spotty or absent by mid-schizonts. Conversely, in PfAPR3-KO parasites, PfAPR4 appeared mislocalized, filling the region enclosed by the basal complex in mid-schizonts (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 9a) before disappearing in late schizonts (Extended Data Fig. 9b). PfCHAKRA–PfAPR3 unidirectional dependency. U-ExM showed that PfCHAKRA was basal to PfAPR3 (Pearson’s R = 0.41). In PfCHAKRAdeficient parasites, proto-APRs were mostly undetectable and PfAPR3 staining was largely absent in mid-schizonts, with only occasional PfAPR3-positive APR rings (2 or 3 per schizont), reflecting residual PfCHAKRA in knockdown. By contrast, PfAPR3 depletion did not affect PfCHAKRA localization at proto-APR in mid-schizonts (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). PfAPR5–PfAPR3 independence. PfAPR5 showed tight spatial overlap with PfAPR3 (Pearson’s R = 0.89), the highest colocalization among APR proteins. In PfAPR5-deficient parasites, PfAPR3 localized normally. Conversely, PfAPR3 depletion also did not affect PfAPR5 localization (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9e). Thus, PfAPR5 and PfAPR3 are not dependent on each other for localization, despite their extremely close colocalization. PfAPR3 and PfAPR4 mutually stabilize each other, while PfAPR5 associates closely with PfAPR3, but neither affects the other’s localization at the APR.

APR biogenesis in P. falciparum While APR assembly in T. gondii proceeds from centrosome-associated arcs to a mature ring structure27, this process is poorly understood in Plasmodium. We tracked PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA localization during schizogony by U-ExM, in which NHS-ester efficiently labels the protein-dense APR, its precursor (proto-APR) and the CP34. The CP is an unconventional centrosome, forming a bipartite structure with distinct extranuclear and intranuclear regions. The extranuclear region is hypothesized to nucleate SPMTs and is physically connected to the proto-APR34,56. Notably, the CP duplicates once per nuclear cycle but is not readily visible at the end of the schizogony34,60–62. Both PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA are recruited to the apical end of the extranuclear CP, forming arc-shaped structures that label the NHS-ester-stained proto-APR. Notably, PfCHAKRA is positioned closer to the proto-APR than PfAPR3, suggesting spatial complexity during APR assembly. As the CP duplicates during the nuclear cycle, the proto-APR, along with PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA, also duplicate, forming paired semi-circles. Maturation into closed APR rings occurred asynchronously; one duplicated CP showed a closed ring-shaped APR, while the other retained an arc-shaped proto-APR. These structures subsequently mature into the closed ring-shaped APRs in the newly formed CPs. At the end of schizogony, when the CP is not visible, the APR ring persisted at the apical end of mature daughter cells, with PfAPR3 remaining associated, whereas PfCHAKRA was no longer visible (Fig. 6a and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Collectively, these results show that APR biogenesis in Plasmodium involves a conserved arc-to-ring maturation, with PfAPR3 and PfCHAKRA occupying distinct spatial positions. While the Plasmodium APR includes three concentric rings6, conventional U-ExM resolved the APR as a single ring. To improve resolution, we applied iterative U-ExM (iU-ExM) with ~15-fold expansion22,63. iU-ExM distinguished two concentric APR rings: a large basal ring and a more apical, dense ring that probably represents the two upper rings merged (Fig. 6b,c and Extended Data Fig. 10b–d). iU-ExM confirmed that PfCHAKRA localizes basal to the PfAPR3 in mid-schizonts (Fig. 6b). Interestingly, PfAPR3 localization differs in mid and late mature schizonts. In late schizonts, PfAPR3 predominantly localized to the largest basal ring (103/103, 100%), whereas in mid-schizonts, it was observed at both basal and apical rings (44/53, 83%). Quantification included 156 APR rings observed from top view across both stages and two biological replicates (Fig. 6c,d).

Discussion In this study, we have identified PfAPR3, PfAPR4, PfCHAKRA and PfAPR5 as essential APR-resident proteins in P. falciparum blood-stage parasites and reveal distinct roles of these components in cytoskeletal organization and host cell invasion. Through live-cell microscopy, we observed that PfAPR3-KO merozoites successfully egress and complete pre-invasion steps but fail to establish a TJ and are unable to invade RBCs. Notably, the RBCs in contact with PfAPR3-KO merozoites showed atypical echinocytosis, characterized by transformation into a rounded sphere with numerous needle-like protrusions. This phenotype closely resembles the effect of R1 treatment, which directly blocks AMA1–RON2 interaction and TJ formation43,64. Taken together, our data suggest that PfAPR3 is required for TJ formation or stabilization, and that its absence phenocopies the effects of direct PfAMA1-RON complex inhibition. Our iU-ExM reveals a spatial and temporal organization of the APR. PfAPR3 localizes to both apical and basal APR rings and physically associates with PfAPR4 and PfAPR5, a complex that persists throughout schizogony. By contrast, PfCHAKRA localizes exclusively to the basal ring during early to mid-schizogony and is absent in late schizonts. The temporal dynamics and distinct functional impacts of these proteins suggest a model in which PfCHAKRA acts as a scaffolding component essential for APR assembly and apical–basal polarization

Methods Plasmid construction and generation of transfected lines PfAPR3DiCre (pPG35). The PfAPR3DiCre parasite strain was generated using a donor plasmid assembled from five PCR-amplified DNA fragments via Golden Gate (GG) assembly with the NEB BsaI-HFv2 kit (E1601L, NEB), following the manufacturer’s protocol. The fragments included the following: (1) the 5′ UTR region, amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with primers oJDD7410/7411; (2) a codon-optimized PfAPR3 gene, amplified from the synthetic gene block GB85 (Biobasic) using oJDD7412/7413; (3) a region containing the linker-3 × HA, LoxP and human dihydrofolate reductase amplified from pPG31 with oJDD7414/7415; (4) the 3′ UTR region, amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD7416/7417; and (5) the pGEM ampicillin region, amplified from plasmid pPG25 using oJDD7418/7419.

PfAPR4iKD (pPG61). The PfAPR4iKD parasite strain was produced by transfecting the donor plasmid pPG61 into the PfAPR3DiCre parasite. The pPG61 plasmid was assembled from five PCR-amplified fragments using GG assembly. The fragments comprised the following: (1) a 5′ homology region (HR) amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD8357/8358, and a codon-optimized PfAPR4 gene from gene block GB100 with oJDD8463/8464 (joined by PCR sewing); (2) smV5, amplified from pPG03 with oJDD8331/8332; (3) TetR-DOZI and blasticidin S deaminase (BSD) cassette, amplified from pPB69 with primers oJDD8333/8334; (4) a 3′ HR region amplified from 3D7 genomic DNA with oJDD8361/8362; and (5) the pGEM backbone, amplified from pPG25 with oJDD8337/8338.

PfCHAKRAiKD (pPG72). The PfCHAKRAiKD parasite strain was generated by integrating the pPG72 construct into the PfAPR3DiCre parasite background. The pPG72 plasmid was assembled from five PCR-amplified fragments using a GG reaction. Image acquisition Z-stacked images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope equipped with Airyscan 2 and a ×63 oil immersion objective. Images were processed by Airyscan processing or joint deconvolution using Zen software and analysed with FIJI72.

U-ExM U-ExM was performed73. Briefly, synchronized parasites were settled on poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips in 24-well plates for 20 min at 37 °C. Parasites were PFA-fixed (4% v/v PBS, 37 °C, 20 min), three times PBS-washed and cross-linked overnight (37 °C; 1.4% v/v formaldehyde + 2% w/v acrylamide in PBS). The next day, gels polymerized in monomer solution (19% sodium acrylate, 10% AA, 0.1% N,N′-methylenebisacrylamide in 10× PBS), TEMED and ammonium persulfate in a pre-chilled gelation chamber (5 min ice; 1 h 37 °C). After polymerization, coverslips and gels were transferred to a 6-well dish containing 1 ml denaturation buffer (200 mM SDS, 200 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris, pH 9) for 15 min with gentle agitation to detach the gels. The detached gel was then incubated with 1.5 ml denaturation buffer in a microcentrifuge tube at 95 °C for 90 min to achieve complete denaturation. Gels were expanded by incubating in 25 ml deionized water (ddH2O) for 30 min at RT (repeated thrice). Gels were PBS-washed (2 × 15 min) and blocked with 3% BSA in PBS for 30 min at RT. Small pieces of gel were cut and incubated with the respective primary antibodies (3% BSA in PBS; overnight at 4 °C). The following day, the gels were washed thrice with 0.5% Tween-20 in PBS for 10 min each and then incubated with secondary antibodies, NHS-ester (for general protein staining) and SYTOX (for nucleic acid staining) for 2.5 h in the dark. The gels were then washed with 0.5% Tween-20 in PBS for 10 min and re-expanded (ddH2O; 30 min). Expanded gels were placed on a poly-D-lysine-coated imaging dish and imaged using a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope with Airyscan 2 and ×40 or ×63 objectives. Images were processed in Zen software and analysed with FIJI72. For colocalization analysis between PfAPR3 and its interacting partners, we manually defined a region of interest (ROI) on fluorescence images using FIJI72 to restrict analysis to the APR region. For each ROI, colocalization between the two channels (PfAPR3 and its interacting partners) was assessed using the Coloc2 plugin. Pearson’s correlation coefficient was calculated to quantify the degree of colocalization with Costes’ automatic thresholding used to minimize background contribution and ensure unbiased analysis. To quantify the angle between two SPMTs in individual schizonts, we used the SNT option of the Neuroanatomy plugin in FIJI for manual tracing74. For each selected pair of SPMTs, the first and last coordinates (x, y and z) of each SPMT were recorded to define their direction vectors. Assuming that the SPMTs were straight lines in three-dimensional space, the angle between the two SPMTs was calculated using the following formula:

Only pairs of SPMTs that were clearly visible and fully traceable throughout their length in each daughter cell were included in the analysis. iU-ExM For iU-ExM22,63,75, PfAPR3DiCre schizonts were Percoll-purified (60%), settled on poly-D-lysine-coated coverslips and fixed with 4% PFA in PBS as U-ExM. The first anchoring step was performed overnight. Monomer solution I (with DHEBA) was added to fill the gelation chamber, followed by incubation on ice (15 min) and polymerization (37 °C, 45 min). Gels were denatured (85 °C, 90 min in buffer) and expanded overnight in water (~5-fold expansion). After expansion, gels were PBS-washed, blocked in 3% BSA, stained with primary and secondary antibodies, and re-expanded with water. For iteration, gels (1.5 cm2) were washed thrice with activated neutral gel and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Gels were subjected to a second round of anchoring solution (37 °C, overnight). The following day, gels were washed in monomer solution III (with BIS) and incubated (37 °C, 1 h). Gels were then washed with 200 mM NaOH (1 h RT), PBS washed until the pH reached 7 and finally expanded overnight in water (~15-fold expansion factor). For imaging, gels were secured (superglue) on poly-D-lysine dishes and imaged with a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope with Airyscan 2 and a ×63 objective. Images were processed using Zen’s Airy-processing software and analysed with FIJI72.

DIC live-cell microscopy For DIC live-cell imaging, 0–2 h synchronized PfAPR3DiCre parasites (5% parasitaemia, 1% HCT) were treated ± 100 nM rapamycin. Percoll-purified schizonts were ML10-arrested (25 nM, BEI Resources) for 2 h before egress. Parasites were washed twice with pre-warmed RPMI, mixed with fresh RBCs and settled in a 35-mm glass-bottom imaging dish (CellView, 627871). Imaging used a Zeiss LSM 980 microscope (DIC prism, ×63 oil) in a pre-warmed microscope chamber. Parasites were imaged every 2.5 s for 30 min. A minimum of three independent biological replicates were performed.

Affinity-based immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry Synchronized PfAPR3DiCre and PfNF54DiCre schizonts (300 ml each, at 3% parasitaemia, 2% HCT; 40–48 hpi) were saponin-released (0.05% saponin in PBS + SigmaFast Protease Inhibitor Cocktail, Sigma). The parasite pellets obtained were resuspended in 1 ml of RIPA lysis buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate and 0.1% SDS) supplemented with protease inhibitors and incubated for 1 h at RT on a rotator. Lysates were then sonicated using a microtip sonicator (20% amplitude, 2 × 30 s on ice, 1 min interval). To remove haemozoin and insoluble debris, lysates were centrifuged (maximum speed, 30 min; 4 °C; Eppendorf 5428). Supernatants were incubated with α-HA (Pierce 88836; overnight 4 °C rotation). After incubation, beads were washed thrice with RIPA in PBS. The beads were subsequently resuspended in 50 μl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and analysed using LC–MS/MS (Taplin Mass Spectrometry core facility at Harvard) on a Thermo Orbitrap mass spectrometer using the data-dependent acquisition mode. Summed intensities for each protein obtained in both sample and control parasites were compared, and proteins with ≥10 unique peptides (n = 2 replicates) were considered for further analysis.

Statistics and reproducibility For all imaging experiments, including slide-based IFA, standard IFA, U-ExM and live-cell imaging, as well as western blot analyses, a minimum of three independent biological replicates were performed to ensure reproducibility. Immunoprecipitation experiments were conducted with two biological replicates. Replication assays were conducted with three independent biological replicates, with each biological replicate including three technical replicates. Results from

all biological replicates, each consisting of technical triplicates, were pooled and presented together in single graphs for analysis. For quantification of schizont and ring-stage parasitaemia by air-dried thin smears, a minimum of 10 random fields was counted per sample, totalling 1,000 cells analysed across 3 independent biological replicates. The angles between two SPMTs were measured in three independent biological replicates. For each biological replicate, 3 schizonts per condition were analysed, with a minimum of 20 pairs of SPMTs per schizont evaluated. Statistical analyses for all experiments were performed using GraphPad Prism software.
